profile.address: 14250 West Broadway Road, Goodyear, Maricopa County, Arizona, 85338
profile.reading: This building is part of Microsoft's Goodyear, Maricopa County, Arizona data center campus, one of three "world-class" campuses (alongside sites in El Mirage) that Governor Doug Ducey and Microsoft announced together on July 31, 2019, representing a combined investment of hundreds of millions of dollars. Microsoft said the campuses would create more than 100 permanent jobs for mechanical engineers, electrical engineers, and data center technicians, plus more than 1,000 temporary construction jobs, and projected roughly $20 million a year in economic impact for the surrounding Arizona communities once operational. The Goodyear campus runs on 100% renewable energy sourced in part from First Solar's 150-megawatt Sun Streams 2 photovoltaic plant, and Microsoft designed the facility for water efficiency such that it uses zero water for much of the year, pursuing LEED Gold certification with a goal of diverting at least 90% of construction waste from landfills. Microsoft has continued expanding the site well past the original 2019 announcement: Data Center Dynamics reported in June 2026 that Microsoft paid $131 million for an additional 100 acres adjacent to its existing 150-acre Goodyear campus, purchased from Chicago-based First Industrial Realty Trust near Citrus and Indian School roads, bringing Microsoft's total Goodyear-area footprint to more than 550 acres; CoStar data cited in that report counted six data center buildings on the campus either existing, under construction, or proposed. The expansion supports Microsoft's West US 3 Azure region, based in Phoenix. Microsoft has separately committed more than $800,000 to Arizona community development and water conservation projects supporting Lake Mead sustainability. Microsoft has not published which of the six campus buildings this specific OSM-mapped structure corresponds to, nor its individual square footage or MW capacity.

profile.campus: Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, California (Microsoft 'BY1-2' data center retrofit, Silicon Valley)
profile.address: 2055 Lafayette Street, Santa Clara, Santa Clara County, California, 95050
profile.reading:
This building at 2055 Lafayette Street in Santa Clara matches the site of what engineering firm BKF Engineers describes as Microsoft's "BY1-2" data center retrofit project, spanning 2045 and 2055 Lafayette Street. BKF, which managed civil engineering, construction management, permitting, stormwater systems, surveying, and utility coordination for the project, described it as transforming a decommissioned facility into a modern, high-capacity data center: a 35.2-megawatt, two-story building comprising two 17.6-megawatt sections, BY1 and BY2, connected by a central electrical room. The retrofit required careful sequencing because certain IT racks and supporting equipment remained live and in service during demolition and reconstruction elsewhere in the building, requiring safety protocols to maintain uninterrupted operation throughout. Microsoft has continued expanding its wider Silicon Valley footprint beyond this retrofit: Data Center Dynamics reported the company purchased 64.5 acres of additional Silicon Valley land while considering a large new data center, and a related project was reported approved by the San Jose Planning Commission. Microsoft's own local.microsoft.com site publishes a California community page and a dedicated "Microsoft datacenters in California" fact sheet, though consistent with its general disclosure practice it does not itemize exact per-building specs there. This Lafayette Street facility's 35.2MW total and 17.6MW-per-section figures, from BKF's own project description, are among the more specific building-level capacity figures found anywhere in this registry for a Microsoft facility, since BKF worked directly on the retrofit rather than relying on aggregator estimates.

Silicon Valley Power, Santa Clara's municipally owned electric utility, supplies power to the city's dense concentration of data centers including Microsoft's Lafayette Street site, and has periodically flagged capacity constraints on its distribution system as a factor data center developers must plan around, a dynamic distinct from investor-owned-utility markets elsewhere in California.

profile.campus: West Des Moines, Iowa (Dallas County portion of Microsoft's multi-campus Azure hub)
profile.address: Grand Avenue, West Des Moines, Boone Township, Dallas County, Iowa, 50266
profile.reading: This building is part of Microsoft's West Des Moines, Iowa data center hub, a cluster of campuses the company has built since first opening in the city in 2012. Microsoft has invested an estimated $5 billion to $6 billion across its West Des Moines facilities to date, per reporting from Wisconsin Public Radio, which visited the site while researching a comparable Microsoft project in Wisconsin, and the company now owns more than 600 acres across the metro. West Des Moines' city engineer told WPR that each Microsoft campus typically comprises three to four buildings and takes roughly eight to ten years to fully build out, which is consistent with this registry finding multiple OSM-mapped Microsoft buildings clustered along the same streets in Dallas, Polk, and Warren counties. More than 600 people now work across Microsoft's West Des Moines data centers, in roles spanning mechanical and electrical engineering, campus management, IT operations, security, and building maintenance, making Microsoft roughly the seventh- or eighth-largest full-time employer in a city of about 73,000 residents. One of the named campuses, internally called Project Osmium, sits on the south side of West Des Moines near Interstate 35; the Business Record has separately reported on a sixth Microsoft data center project, called Project Ruthenium, planned near Veterans Parkway and Woodland Avenue with an initial $210 million, 245,000-square-foot building and roughly 25 permanent jobs, part of a site that could eventually hold up to four buildings. This building sits along Grand Avenue or Booneville Road in Dallas County, in the western portion of Microsoft's West Des Moines footprint; Microsoft has not published which named campus or project this specific building belongs to, nor its individual square footage or MW capacity, consistent with the company's general practice of not disclosing per-building specifics for its Azure data centers.

This building is part of Microsoft's Quincy, Grant County, Washington data center campus, the company's original Central Washington site and now, per GeekWire's reporting from a May 2026 20th-anniversary celebration, the anchor of what has become Washington's largest data center hub, with Microsoft as the largest operator among several tech companies that have since built there. Microsoft first opened in Quincy around 2006, drawn by what was then surplus, low-cost hydropower from the Columbia River system; GeekWire reported that advantage has diminished over the two decades since as regional droughts became more frequent, prompting Grant County's public utility district to plan roughly $260 million in new transmission line investment, toward which Microsoft has committed more than $2.6 million. At the 20th-anniversary event Microsoft awarded $210,000 in grants to local organizations, on top of the property tax revenue its campus has generated over two decades that GeekWire reported helped fund a new high school and police station in Quincy; the town's poverty rate more than halved over the ten years through 2023, dropping to 13%, a change local and national coverage (including Fox News and OPB) have both linked substantially to Microsoft's and other data center operators' presence. Roughly 350 full-time Microsoft employees work across the Quincy data center campus, a workforce nearly seven times the size of the newer, smaller East Wenatchee campus Microsoft built in neighboring Douglas County starting in 2022. Microsoft has not published which specific building on the multi-structure Quincy campus this OSM-mapped way corresponds to, nor its individual square footage or MW capacity.

Grant County PUD, the public utility district serving Quincy, has structured its roughly $260 million transmission expansion as a cost-sharing arrangement with its largest data center customers rather than spreading the full cost across residential ratepayers, with Microsoft's multi-million-dollar contribution reported as one of several such large-load agreements the district has negotiated as Columbia Basin data center demand has grown beyond what the original hydropower surplus could support.

profile.campus: Cheyenne, Laramie County, Wyoming (Microsoft Azure data center operations since 2012)
profile.address: Horizon Drive, Laramie County, Wyoming, 82005
profile.reading:
This building is part of Microsoft's Cheyenne, Laramie County, Wyoming data center operations, where Microsoft has operated since 2012 and now employs approximately 320 full-time staff. Microsoft's own newsroom announced in April 2026 its intent to purchase roughly 3,200 acres across two parcels south and near Cheyenne for major new data center development, 200 acres in Bison Business Park and about 3,000 acres in Southeast Cheyenne, which local and trade press including Cowboy State Daily described as roughly tripling Microsoft's existing Cheyenne footprint; Microsoft said the expansion would follow a multiyear planning and development process including public hearings and community engagement before construction begins. In 2025, Microsoft's existing Cheyenne facilities generated more than $11 million in local property taxes, making the company Cheyenne's top taxpayer and Laramie County's second-largest. Microsoft has committed more than $68 million in completed and planned local infrastructure improvements, including roadway upgrades, water infrastructure, and storm sewer enhancements, and has donated $4.7 million across 56 community projects since 2018. The company's Datacenter Academy at Laramie County Community College has trained more than 1,000 students since 2019 for data center careers. Microsoft has pledged to offset the expansion's electricity consumption with carbon-free energy and to replenish more water than its Cheyenne operations consume through partnerships with local conservation organizations. Microsoft has not published this specific building's individual square footage or MW capacity, consistent with its general practice of not disclosing per-building specifics for its Azure data centers.

Cheyenne Light, Fuel and Power, the local utility, and the Wyoming Public Service Commission have both been named in local coverage of Microsoft's proposed 3,200-acre expansion as parties the company will need to work with on power delivery for the new campus, and Wyoming state officials have highlighted the project as part of the state's broader push to diversify its historically energy-and-minerals-dependent economy toward data infrastructure.
